These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cognitive performance is used as a proxy for work performance and safety. This meta -analysis and systematic review compared cognitive performance during night shifts (23:00–07:00) with daytime performance (07:00–23:00) across experimental field and laboratory studies, excluding shifts exceeding 24 h. Meta-regressions examined night shift, study context, and cognitive test characteristics as sources of heterogeneity. Fifty-five studies were included, yielding 758 night work and 964 daytime datapoints from 1,919 participants, combined into 6135 effect sizes. Cognitive performance was impaired during night shifts relative to daytime hours (Hedges g = −0.36, 95% CI [−0.49, −0.23], p < 0.001), although indications of publication bias suggest this pooled estimate is somewhat inflated. Impairments increased with time into the shift, from 0:01–08:59 h (g = −0.33, 95% CI [−0.63, −0.02], p = 0.041) to > 9 h (g = −0.61, 95% CI [−0.96, −0.25], p = 0.004). Impairments were more pronounced on simple tests (g = −0.50, 95% CI [−0.70, −0.31], p < 0.001), as complex tests weakened the night-daytime difference (g = 0.29, 95% CI [0.07, 0.50], p < 0.001). This contrast was driven by the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT); excluding PVT data removed the difference and attenuated the pooled effect to g = −0.24. No significant moderating effects emerged for time point during the shift, shift sequence, test outcome, or study context (field vs. laboratory). Extended night shifts thus appear detrimental to safety, with heightened sensitivity concentrated in psychomotor vigilance type tasks. Both contexts appear valid for examining these effects. Remaining heterogeneity warrants further investigation of environmental and individual factors.

Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

This study examines how North Korean youth who used smartphones before defecting negotiated privacy, autonomy, and everyday agency under device-embedded surveillance, termed here the ‘mobile panopticon’. It combines Giorgi’s descriptive phenomenology, applied to interviews with nine defectors, with an Actor-Network Theory (ANT) analysis of technical reports, legal texts, and participants’ accounts. The study reveals how circumvention of surveillance carved out private autonomy, de-monopolised cognitive horizons, and renegotiated biographical trajectories, held together by fear and transgressive pleasure. A heuristic three-phase periodisation – ‘open window’ (2008–2013), ‘walled garden’ (2014–2017), and ‘beyond the wall’ (2018 onward) – shows the state’s efforts at enclosure extending from device architecture into law, while users moved from ‘side gates’ and ‘breaches’ to media outside the handset. Integrating both layers, the study proposes ‘embodied sociotechnical agency’, comprising embodied interiority, sociotechnical buffering, and agency reconfiguration, and shows how circumvention became, for some participants, a condition of counter-conduct. The findings characterise this defector subgroup, not North Korean youth as a whole, and extend Scott’s ideas of hidden transcripts and Foucauldian counter-conduct to device-embedded surveillance.
topics: Korean Peninsula Historical and Political Studies

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.

Abstract Genomic foundation models provide transferable DNA sequence representations, but their application to sample-level classification requires effective integration of sequencing reads. We present EvoGR (Evo 2-based Genomic Representation), a read-level transfer framework using a shared frozen Evo 2 encoder and Permutation-invariant Attention Aggregation (PAA). Mean pooling converts variable-length single-stranded reads into fixed-dimensional embeddings, while PAA integrates variable-sized, unordered read sets. EvoGR addresses two complementary tasks: population classification using AIM-enriched reads and four-class genome-origin classification involving human, non-human animal, plant, and microorganism sequences. Inference requires only single-stranded reads, without reference genomes, SNP coordinates, or explicit REF/ALT representations. EvoGR achieved competitive performance across both tasks and maintained strong classification performance on real human sequencing data, demonstrating transfer from simulated to real sequencing inputs. Comparisons across genomic foundation models identified Evo 2 as the strongest encoder under the evaluated settings. Ablation experiments demonstrated the contribution of PAA, while read-length sensitivity analyses showed that longer reads generally improved classification performance, with diminishing gains at greater lengths. These findings establish EvoGR as a unified framework for read-level genomic representation transfer across distinct biological classification tasks.

This study investigated students' behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement, and their perceived effectiveness of Wordwall, following the use of Wordwall activities in English sentence construction lessons in one secondary school in Malaysia. While digital and game-based learning are gaining traction in the language classroom, constructing sentences can be a challenge for language learners and may need to be practised multiple times with feedback and active engagement. A quantitative descriptive survey design was employed with 55 Form 1 and Form 2 students from four classes in one secondary school in Malaysia. The participants engaged in three Wordwall-based sentence construction sessions followed by a post-intervention questionnaire that measured behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement and the perceived effectiveness of Wordwall. The data were analysed using frequencies, means, standard deviations and Cronbach's alpha to assess the internal consistency of the questionnaire scales. The results showed that self-reported engagement scores were moderately positive across all three dimensions, with emotional engagement recording the highest mean score (M = 3.45, SD = 0.85), followed by cognitive engagement (M = 3.42, SD = 0.82) and behavioural engagement (M = 3.34, SD = 0.84); however, differences among the three dimensions were small. Students also reported moderately positive perceptions of the effectiveness of Wordwall for learning sentence construction (M = 3.28, SD = 1.09). These findings suggest that Wordwall may serve as a supplementary tool in interactive and participatory sentence construction lessons. However, the study did not measure learning gains, no control group was used, and the small convenience sample limits generalisation; the results therefore reflect students' self-reported perceptions only. Future research should incorporate objective measures of learning and stronger comparative designs in ESL classrooms. Kajian ini meneliti penglibatan tingkah laku, emosi dan kognitif pelajar serta persepsi mereka terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall susulan penggunaan aktiviti Wordwall dalam pengajaran pembinaan ayat bahasa Inggeris di sebuah sekolah menengah di Malaysia. Walaupun pembelajaran digital dan pembelajaran berasaskan permainan semakin mendapat tempat dalam bilik darjah bahasa, pembinaan ayat boleh menjadi cabaran kepada pelajar dan mungkin memerlukan latihan berulang dengan maklum balas serta penglibatan aktif. Reka bentuk tinjauan deskriptif kuantitatif digunakan melibatkan 55 orang pelajar Tingkatan 1 dan Tingkatan 2 daripada empat kelas di sebuah sekolah menengah di Malaysia. Peserta kajian mengambil bahagian dalam tiga sesi pembinaan ayat berasaskan Wordwall yang diikuti dengan soal selidik pascaintervensi untuk mengukur penglibatan tingkah laku, emosi dan kognitif serta persepsi terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall. Data dianalisis menggunakan kekerapan, min, sisihan piawai dan alfa Cronbach bagi menilai ketekalan dalaman skala soal selidik tersebut. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa skor penglibatan yang dilaporkan sendiri oleh pelajar berada pada tahap sederhana positif merentasi ketiga-tiga dimensi, dengan penglibatan emosi mencatatkan skor min tertinggi (M = 3.45, SD = 0.85), diikuti oleh penglibatan kognitif (M = 3.42, SD = 0.82) dan penglibatan tingkah laku (M = 3.34, SD = 0.84). Walau bagaimanapun, perbezaan antara ketiga-tiga dimensi tersebut adalah kecil. Pelajar juga melaporkan persepsi yang sederhana positif terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall dalam pembelajaran pembinaan ayat (M = 3.28, SD = 1.09). Dapatan ini menunjukkan bahawa Wordwall berpotensi digunakan sebagai alat sokongan dalam pengajaran pembinaan ayat secara interaktif dan melibatkan penyertaan aktif pelajar. Namun demikian, kajian ini tidak mengukur peningkatan hasil pembelajaran, tiada kumpulan kawalan digunakan, dan saiz sampel mudah yang kecil membataskan kebolehumuman dapatan. Oleh itu, dapatan kajian ini hanya mencerminkan persepsi yang dilaporkan sendiri oleh pelajar. Kajian pada masa hadapan wajar menggunakan pengukuran hasil pembelajaran secara objektif serta reka bentuk kajian perbandingan yang lebih kukuh dalam bilik darjah bahasa Inggeris sebagai bahasa kedua (ESL).

High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Process-based terrestrial biosphere models such as the Ecosystem Demography (ED) model underpin global carbon budgets, but their cost limits global, high-resolution and scenario-rich simulation. Deep emulators such as DeepED reduce that cost but require task-specific architectures and training. Tabular foundation models offer a different route: TabPFN predicts new rows by in-context learning, without being trained on the task. We compare TabPFN-3.5 with two DeepED baselines, $DeepED_{LSTM}$ and $DeepED_{Transformer}$, on CarbonGlobe's overall evaluation, which trains on a uniform 1/16 sample of sites and tests on the other 50,779, predicting the 40-year state of all seven ED outputs. We then test every model, trained on present-day data only, on ED runs forced by SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 for 2021--2060 in six continental forest regions. With no training, TabPFN-3.5 has the lowest present-day height error of the three models and is within 4% of $DeepED_{LSTM}$ for soil carbon, but is less accurate for AGB, LAI and the carbon fluxes. In 2060, errors are several times larger than at the same sites under present-day forcing, and every model underestimates the biomass that ED gains. Under SSP5-8.5, TabPFN-3.5 is the most accurate model for height, AGB, soil carbon and LAI, with the lowest AGB error in all six regions, although, unlike ED, it predicts no larger biomass gain than under SSP1-2.6. Under SSP1-2.6, no model is best overall.
topics: Plant Water Relations and Carbon Dynamics

documents.abstract: Technological advancements are transforming warehouse operations, as robotic solutions are increasingly deployed to enhance efficiency and productivity. Although these technologies reduce physical strain and automate repetitive tasks, their broader effects on human factors (HFs), including perceptual, mental, physical, and psychosocial dimensions, remain insufficiently understood. Moreover, explicit links between specific robotic capabilities and task-level effects on workers remain limited. To address this gap, this study develops a human-centric, task-level framework for evaluating how different robotic solutions influence HFs in warehouse operations. Using an exploratory, qualitative, multi-method approach, the study triangulates insights from literature, practitioner discussions, robotics solution providers, and end users to classify robotic solutions according to interaction level, task-execution roles, and adaptability. Application of the framework to the key warehouse task of order picking shows that robotic solutions reduce physical workload while introducing mixed mental and perceptual demands related to supervision and monitoring, and psychosocial challenges associated with shared-space interaction and job engagement. These findings highlight the importance of early human-centric evaluation during technology selection and implementation, enabling organisations to anticipate potential benefits and challenges prior to deployment. The framework supports human-centric decision-making in warehouse robotics and provides a basis for future empirical research on task-level human–robot interaction (HRI).

topics: Inclusion and Disability in Education and Sport

documents.abstract: The digitalization of teaching has become a global educational priority aimed at enhancing student engagement and promoting learner-centered instruction.In Rwanda, national initiatives such as the ICT in Education Policy and Smart Classroom Project seek to integrate digital technologies into classroom practices.However, limited evidence exists regarding teachers' perceptions of digitalization and its influence on student engagement at the school level.This qualitative case study explored secondary school teachers' perceptions of the digitalization of teaching and its influence on students' behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement at GS Kagugu in Gasabo District, Rwanda.Guided by Constructivist Learning Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study employed an interpretivist paradigm using semi-structured interviews and document analysis.Five purposively selected teachers from different subject areas participated in the study.Thematic analysis revealed that teachers conceptualize digitalization either as the substitution of traditional instructional tools or as a pedagogical transformation that promotes learner-centered and interactive learning.The findings indicated that digital teaching practices positively influence student motivation, participation, attention, and conceptual understanding when effectively integrated.However, challenges including unstable internet connectivity, power interruptions, limited digital competencies, and inadequate professional development constrain meaningful technology integration.The study recommends continuous school-based professional development, peer-led mentoring initiatives, equitable access to digital resources, and the provision of localized offline-capable digital learning materials.Educational digitalization should therefore prioritize teacher capacity building alongside technological investments to maximize student engagement and learning outcomes.

For decades, the nation’s largest provider of forensic proficiency tests, Collaborative Testing Services, structured its firearms examination exercises around bullet and cartridge case comparisons so simplistic as to nearly guarantee vanishingly low misidentification rates. Practitioners, in turn, enthusiastically relied on these results during increasingly vigorous admissibility challenges to defend their alleged ability—using little more than their training, experience, and subjective judgment—to divine the precise gun used in a crime. By and large, they succeeded. Although outside scholars (lawyers, statisticians, human factors experts, and more) have remained constant in their criticisms of the field’s methods and the design of its efforts to measure accuracy (in the form of proficiency testing and beyond), untroubled admissibility and untroubled qualification of firearms examiners as “experts” have remained the norm. In 2023, however, CTS (albeit unintentionally) bucked the trend of simplistic testing, releasing an exercise, CTS 23–5262, that forced participants to confront damaged and poorly marked bullets. The results should trouble even those unfamiliar with firearms examination and the debates about its validity. Although the questioned bullets provided to participants were not fired by the same gun as the exemplar bullets in their packets, 22% of test takers failed by “matching” at least one questioned item to the exemplars, and participants on the whole committed misidentifications 37.4% of the time they offered definitive conclusions about the source of the “challenging” bullets in the proficiency test. To highlight the importance of these results, and to emphasize the extent they depart from past proficiency tests, this Article both analyzes CTS bullet exercises dating back to 2006 and dives deeply into CTS 23–5262 itself. Examiners’ performance failures on the latter, this Article ultimately argues, (1) contradict claims that analysts will rarely err when assessing the source of fired ammunition; (2) raise questions about the validity of comparisons performed on damaged bullets; and (3) force litigants and the courts to grapple with the significance of test error when qualifying individual examiners as experts. Indeed, given how grossly CTS 23–5262 runs counter to the claims made by defenders of firearms examination (and the judges who have parroted them), it may be that the test can (or at least should) finally push the field over the edge and out of criminal courts.

Communicating conservation science to children requires transforming highly technical documentation into accessible, engaging, and scientifically reliable narratives. This paper presents a human in the loop framework that formalizes conservation documentation as epistemic ground truth and employs Generative AI exclusively for controlled narrative adaptation. The conservator retains full editorial authority, ensuring epistemic reliability and ethical compliance. The methodology is demonstrated through three comparative case studies implemented on freely-accessible/no-code platforms, Animaker, Genially, and Lumi Education/H5P, representing animated storytelling with puzzles, interactive flip card discovery, and quiz based reinforcement. The paper outlines future directions for evaluating the clarity and accessibility of the digital narratives within museum contexts. As part of an ongoing doctoral dissertation, the work outlines core research questions, methodological milestones, and future directions, including the release of an open repository to support reproducibility. The framework contributes a scalable, low-barrier model for responsible AI-assisted communication of conservation knowledge in museum contexts.

Introduction: Student motivation influences learners’ willingness to initiate, sustain and complete academic tasks. Gamification introduces selected game-design elements into instruction and may influence both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Purpose: This study examined the effect of gamification on the intrinsic and extrinsic motivation of Senior Secondary School One (SS1) students in Enugu North Local Government Area, Enugu State, Nigeria. Methodology: A quasi-experimental, non-equivalent control-group design was used with 160 SS1 students from four public secondary schools. Eighty students were assigned to the experimental group and 80 to the control group. The experimental group received four weeks of instruction incorporating points, badges, leaderboards, challenges and feedback, while the control group received conventional instruction. Data were collected with the Students’ Motivation Questionnaire and analysed using means, standard deviations and independent-samples t-tests. Results: The experimental group recorded higher reported mean scores than the control group for intrinsic motivation (3.52 versus 2.81), t(158) = 6.90, p < .001, and extrinsic motivation (3.50 versus 2.87), t(158) = 6.22, p < .001. Conclusion: The group comparisons indicate that students exposed to gamified instruction reported higher intrinsic- and extrinsic-motivation scores than students receiving conventional instruction. Recommendation: Teachers should align game elements with learning objectives and combine recognition and rewards with meaningful challenges, learner choice and informative feedback.

This study challenges the assumption that distributive justice remains a dominant driver of employee retention in resource‑constrained contexts. Drawing on Organizational Justice Theory, Self‑Determination Theory, and Two‑Factor Theory, the research examines how job satisfaction, work–life balance, distributive justice, and perceived job quality influence employees’ intention to stay within a private sector healthcare environment. The study investigates whether distributive fairness still remains a dominant driver of retention in an economically constrained environment. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‑SEM) on survey data from 177 employees across multiple settings, results indicate that job satisfaction and work–life balance significantly predict intention to stay, whereas distributive justice and perceived job quality do not. The findings suggest that intrinsic motivational factors tend to supersede distributive fairness considerations in a limited resourced context, thereby offering boundary conditions for justice‑based retention frameworks. Its implications for contextualized HRM theory and retention strategy are further discussed.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as the technology that will allow green human resource management (GHRM) to deliver organizational sustainability, yet the evidence behind this claim is recent, scattered and largely unexamined. This study combines a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review with a VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis to establish what is known, how it is known and what remains untested. A Scopus search (12 November 2026) returned 297 records; after document-type filtering and title–abstract–keyword screening, 97 journal articles and reviews formed the mapping corpus, and two further eligible articles were added to the critical synthesis (n = 99). Keyword co-occurrence, overlay, co-citation, bibliographic coupling and country co-authorship maps were produced, and every study was coded for the structural role assigned to AI, theory, method, context and outcome. The field is young (77.3% of the corpus is published from 2025–2026), geographically limited (mostly emerging Asian countries), and methodologically homogeneous, with 44 of 62 quantitative studies using cross-sectional structural equation modelling of self-reported data. Five roles for AI are discussed (enabler, amplifier, mediator, complementary resource and embedded practice), but they are often mixed up, or not well explained theoretically. The conceptual foundations are the resource-based view and the GHRM foundations and the critical literature on algorithmic management is not present in the co-citation structure. These are flanked by reports in other studies of non-significant and negative effects, as well as no environmental footprint for AI itself, meaning the current optimism is premature. The paper introduces a typology of AI roles and a socio-technical capability-conversion framework that consists of six propositions, and a research agenda.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.

Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter closes the book with an argument for New Materialist Informatics as a transdisciplinary critical technical practice. It discusses the diagrammatics of machine learning as a framework of knowledge production as well as of power in machine learning systems. Positioning machine learning systems as complex assemblages, the chapter argues that the analysis and design of such systems require transdisciplinary critical approaches. A synthetic field of New Materialist Informatics is introduced as one such transdisciplinary practice, which brings together research and epistemology of new materialisms together with sociotechnical design practices. A method of transposition is proposed as a way to activate feminist new materialist conceptual foundations for technical practice.

Financial critical infrastructures face mounting cyber threats across heterogeneous, fragmented digital ecosystems. Existing Security Operations Centre architectures, spanning SIEM platforms, XDR systems, and threat intelligence feeds, lack the contextual reasoning, governance alignment, and explainability that highly regulated environments require. We propose a trustworthy multi-agent cybersecurity architecture that integrates LLM-enhanced contextual orchestration grounded in shared semantic security knowledge, human-in-the-loop governance, compliance-aware runtime control, and collaborative threat intelligence. Rather than treating cyber resilience as a purely technical detection problem, our framework conceptualises it as a socio-technical orchestration challenge explicitly designed to support compliance with DORA, NIS2, GDPR, PSD2, and the EU AI Act. We describe a six-layer architecture, analyse its governance and resilience implications, and identify open research challenges. The central argument is that AI agents should augment cybersecurity professionals, not replace them, preserving human authority over high-stakes decisions while reducing alert fatigue and enabling privacy-preserving collaborative defence across institutions.

Objective This study examined trust contagion and trust transfer in co-located multi-human multi-Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) teams and adopted the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) to model trust dynamics in human-autonomy teams (HAT). Background Most HAT research has focused on dyadic relationships, yet real-world operations increasingly involve multiple human operators collaborating with multiple agents. How trust spreads between human teammates and transfers across agents in non-dyadic contexts remains poorly understood. Method A 3 (UAV reliability: High-High, Mixed, Low-Low; within-subjects) × 2 (Priming: Trust vs. Distrust; between-subjects) mixed design was used. Fifty-three dyads ( N = 106) performed a target acquisition task in two-human, two-UAV teams. Subjective trust was analyzed using linear mixed models as the primary analysis, with APIM as a secondary exploratory analysis of dyadic influence. Results For trust contagion, UAV reliability was the primary driver of trust, with no evidence that primed attitudes spread between operators, suggesting boundary conditions on when contagion occurs. For trust transfer, trust in the reliable UAV did not decline when paired with an unreliable one, supporting component-specific trust. Exploratory APIM helped disentangle dyadic interdependence and generate hypotheses for future work. Conclusion Trust in multi-human multi-agent teams was driven primarily by system reliability, with operators adopting component-specific trust, calibrating trust to each UAV individually. Application Supporting calibrated trust depends first on system reliability and on direct experience with each agent’s performance. APIM offers a means to distinguish an operator’s own trust development from a teammate’s influence, making it suited to studying trust in multi-human multi-agent teams.

Abstract The construction industry is a hazardous sector characterized by high rates of accidents, injuries, and work-related disability. To inform a comprehensive approach to disability-related issues, this study examines research trends on disability in the construction sector and proposes future research directions. A total of 623 articles on disability in construction from the Web of Science and Scopus databases were analyzed using latent Dirichlet allocation topic modeling. Fifteen topics were identified and categorized into three thematic areas: (1) Ergonomic Exposure, Outcomes, and Interventions for Musculoskeletal Disorders, (2) Occupational Hazards and Health Outcomes, and (3) Disability Management and Transition Support. Drawing upon the biopsychosocial model, the findings reveal that existing research has predominantly focused on biological dimensions, with limited integration of psychological and social dimensions. This review identifies critical gaps, including limited attention to how emerging technologies reshape work processes, insufficient understanding of the links between early functional indicators and long-term disability outcomes, and a lack of research on career transitions and preemployment contexts. The findings highlight the need for anticipatory and longitudinal research that integrates biological, psychological, and social dimensions and connects exposure, functional capacity, and return-to-work trajectories. Practically, the results underscore the importance of integrated interventions and improved systems for early intervention, rehabilitation, and sustained workforce participation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Care is primarily a collective phenomenon, with a practice that involves sharing health and wellbeing information within a trusted “care circle” of family members and companions for sensemaking, interpretation, decision-making, and follow-through. However, current digital health tools and information systems are designed for individuals and primarily intended for Personal Health Informatics (PHI). This mismatch between collective practice and individualistic design creates new challenges for the proactive use of such systems in care settings and limits adoption, sustained engagement, and meaningful use. To examine how people practice collective care and how (if) they perceive, adopt, and integrate PHI systems for proactive care, we conducted a sequential mixed-methods study. Through an initial survey (n=87) and semi-structured interviews (n=22), we found that their practices involve collectively understanding, analyzing, and sensemaking health information. However, we also found that their use of existing systems to support such practices is constrained by factors at personal, relational, technological, and structural levels that evolve over time. To address these constraints and explore redesigning PHI toward “Collective Health Informatics”, we conducted eight stakeholder interview sessions with 12 participants, a follow-up survey (n=114), and six co-design workshops with 12 participants to understand the dynamics required in collective settings while retaining agency. Using a design probe evaluation (n=38), we refine a design vision for coordinated, trustworthy action across such care relationships. Our findings motivate CC-Proact , an operational map that translates ecological influences into three design levers: Agency , Elicitation , and Engagement . Using this map, our work empirically examines collective care practices and offers six design recommendations to build responsible systems that proactively support collective care.

In an era of growing data volumes, advances in data storage and processing technologies have created a landscape in which organizations — whether commercial, government, or educational — increasingly request analytical methods that convert raw data into valuable, actionable insights and knowledge. This research employed Data Mining (DM) techniques — including text mining and social network analysis — and Machine Learning (ML) methods, specifically hierarchical agglomerative and K-means clustering, and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for topic modeling, to support knowledge discovery across 287 scientific publications focused on information management and data insights. Main findings include: artificial intelligence and machine learning were the most common bigrams in titles; five clusters were identified, with cluster C1 containing the five most cited articles; LDA modeling identified six topics, with Topic 6, Machine Learning/Deep Learning and Predictive Modeling, containing 59 articles on technical and algorithmic aspects. This work could motivate researchers in Data, Information, and Management to deepen their understanding of the field, guide strategic academic development, and promote new knowledge and scientific advances within the discipline.

Image-to-3D foundation models have improved 3D reconstruction, but typically produce monolithic representations without explicit part-level structure. Part-aware generation and learning-based assembly methods often require part-level supervision, category-specific priors, or paired part-layout training data. We instead consider a practical but underexplored setting in which independently prepared or generated 3D parts have no predefined inter-part relationships, shared coordinate frames, or consistent scales, and must be assembled into a reference-consistent object from a single image. We present VA-Assembly, a training-free framework for 3D part assembly through part-level transformation estimation using view-aligned diffusion guidance. Given a reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly optimizes each part's translation, rotation, and scale. We condition a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D representation, producing score gradients geometrically aligned with the part configuration. This guidance provides multi-view structural cues under large initial misalignment. By repurposing pretrained visual-structural priors as transformation-level supervision, VA-Assembly requires no annotated part layouts, predefined part taxonomies, category-specific assembly training, or bounding-box-based layout initialization. Experiments compare VA-Assembly with geometric registration and compositional layout baselines using each baseline's supported transformation components, showing improved part-wise transformation estimation. Ablation studies show that view-aligned conditioning, rather than diffusion guidance alone, is critical for reliable transformation gradients. Updating only part transformations preserves explicit component separability and supports component-level editing, replacement, and reconfiguration.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.

Background: Collaborative learning in medical education relies on both social integration and cognitive engagement. The classroom community scale (CCS) measures students’ sense of community through two dimensions: Connectedness and learning. In German-speaking countries, the CCS has previously been validated in its full form (CCS-D). While an English short form (CCS-SF) exists, a validated German short form for efficient assessment was lacking. This study aimed to develop and validate a short form of the German CCS (CCS-D-SF). Methods: The CCS-D was systematically reduced to a ten-item short form using principal component analysis (PCA) and iterative reliability analysis. Data on the short form were collected from N=171 first-semester medical students at the University of Tuebingen. Internal consistency was evaluated with Cronbach’s alpha. Construct validity was assessed using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and PCA. Results: The CCS-D-SF retained a two-factor structure corresponding to connectedness (i=5) and learning (i=5). The total scale showed good internal consistency (α=.81), with reliability for the subscales connectedness (α=.86) and learning (α=.65). CFA indicated an acceptable model fit (χ2/df=2.16, RMSEA=.083, SRMR=.059, CFI=.93, TLI=.91), and PCA displayed also the factor structure. Discussion: The CCS-D-SF is a valid, and practical instrument for assessing sense of community among German-speaking first-year medical students. Reliability ranges from marginal for learning to very good for connectedness. The overall reliability can be considered to be good. Questionnaires brevity reduces respondent burden without compromising psychometric quality and makes it suitable for educational research and classroom diagnostics. The CCS-D-SF may also inform interventions aiming to strengthen both social integration and learning engagement in collaborative medical education settings.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming intelligent transportation systems by connecting roadside cameras, edge computing units, vehicles, and traffic infrastructure into a shared sensing and decision-making ecosystem. However, transmitting raw traffic video over vehicle-to-everything (V2X) links is bandwidth-intensive, while deploying large multimodal models directly on resource-constrained vehicles is often impractical. To address these limitations, this article proposes VISTA (Vision-Informed Semantic Traffic Awareness), a multimodal vision-language edge-intelligence framework that combines predictive video representation learning with lightweight language-based reasoning to provide communication-efficient traffic situational awareness. In the proposed architecture, roadside surveillance units employ the Video Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) and an attentive-pooler module to convert traffic video clips into compact future-scene embeddings. These embeddings are transmitted through V2X links to vehicle-mounted systems, where a TinyLlama small language model, enhanced with a custom visual adapter, interprets the embeddings alongside natural-language (NL) traffic queries. VISTA enables vehicles to obtain interpretable traffic information, reason about upcoming scene dynamics, and identify potential collision risks without receiving raw video streams. Experimental results in a digital-twin urban traffic environment show that VISTA achieves 97.77% accuracy and an 89% F1 score for future collision prediction while reducing the communication payload by several orders of magnitude compared with raw RGB video transmission. These results demonstrate the feasibility of embedding-based multimodal intelligence for low-latency, communication-efficient, and safety-oriented IoT-enabled transportation systems.

Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

As symptom checkers based on artificial intelligence (AI) are becoming common entry points for health information, their influence on lay users' diagnostic decisions raises questions about trust and bias. Of particular concern is confirmation bias, the tendency to favour information that supports one's existing belief while discounting information that contradicts it. One of the central design choices for such systems is the style of voice: whether they should present themselves with a human-like (anthropomorphic) or a clearly machine-like (xenomorphic) voice. This study investigates whether the voice design of an AI symptom checker modulates confirmation bias in self-diagnosis. In a within-subjects online experiment (N = 81 participants, 648 trials), participants selected a diagnosis and rated their confidence, then heard an AI-generated recommendation that either confirmed or contradicted their initial choice, delivered by an anthropomorphic or a machine-like voice, before deciding again. We observed a strong, direction-dependent influence of the AI: participants revised their diagnosis in 45.7% of trials when the AI contradicted them versus 1.2% when it confirmed them (generalised linear mixed model, GLMM, p < .001); confidence rose under confirmation but barely moved under contradiction (robust linear mixed model, p < .001); and decisions took longer after contradiction (Gamma GLMM, p < .001). This effect did not differ between the two voices (no voice or interaction term was significant, smallest p = .282), even though a manipulation check confirmed the voices were perceived as markedly different. The findings suggest that the direction of an AI recommendation, rather than the anthropomorphism of its voice, drives confirmation-related bias in AI-assisted self-diagnosis.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments across diverse CLIP architectures, more than 30 visual benchmarks, generative backbones, and MLLMs consistently validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation, establishing a new benchmark for visual representation learning.

Test-time augmentation (TTA) aggregates model predictions across multiple transformed views of an input during inference. Because histology images lack a canonical orientation, $D_4$ TTA---pooling across the 8 rotations and reflections of a square---is a standard default in computational pathology. However, the rise of self-supervised histology foundation models (FMs) with inherent rotational invariance calls its continued utility into question. We benchmark 9 histology FMs and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image (WSI) datasets. We find that $D_4$ TTA remains a reliable post hoc improvement, but benefits diminish from $+1.98$ percentage points (pp) for general-purpose backbones to $+0.50$ pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT, and shrink further for the largest models. To eliminate computational overhead, our experiments demonstrate that entropy routing---applying TTA selectively to uncertain predictions---recovers most of the gain while augmenting only ${\sim}13\%$ of samples. Finally, we show that patch-level TTA improvements do not transfer to slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL). Code: https://github.com/lars-chen/histology-tta
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how researchers encounter and make sense of scholarly information. By producing coherent explanations from multiple sources, these systems may influence how users assess their understanding, evaluate supporting evidence, and decide whether further investigation is necessary. This project investigates how AI-generated scholarly synthesis shapes judgments of explanatory and evidentiary sufficiency in academic research. Its central question is whether, and under what conditions, the perceived completeness of an explanation influences a researcher’s assessment of the evidence supporting it and their decision to continue or conclude an information search. The research draws on library and information science, human-computer interaction, epistemology, and cognitive psychology. It examines established accounts of information satisficing, search stopping behavior, cognitive authority, epistemic dependence, and metacognitive calibration to assess how these concepts explain information-seeking decisions in AI-mediated environments. A central distinction concerns the difference between understanding an explanation and having sufficient grounds to accept its claims. These judgments may coincide, but they need not. An explanation may adequately address a research question while leaving important uncertainties about source quality, methodological limitations, or competing interpretations unresolved. Conversely, reliance on a well-supported synthesis may be entirely justified without extensive examination of every underlying source. Rather than treating reduced information seeking as an inherent failure, the project considers how researchers determine when further inquiry is warranted. It examines the conditions under which AI-generated synthesis may support well-calibrated judgments, encourage critical engagement with evidence, or contribute to premature conclusions. The project aims to develop a theoretically grounded account of evidentiary judgment and inquiry termination in AI-mediated scholarly research, with implications for information literacy, scholarly information practices, and the design of research support systems.

Why does meaningful work become inaccessible to certain groups? Existing literature increasingly recognizes that access to meaningful work is shaped by both subjective experiences and objective conditions, yet it remains less clear about how and why such access becomes systematically constrained. In particular, prior studies tend to foreground workers’ active agency in engaging with, negotiating or resisting these conditions of meaningful work, but they offer limited insight into how this capacity itself may be restricted. Drawing on Archer’s distinction between active and passive agency, we conceptualize passive agency as a mechanism through which structural constraints limit workers’ capability for purposive action. Based on 33 interviews with disabled workers in China, we show how ableism acts as a structural constraint, positioning disabled workers as passive agents, restricting their capacity to experience work as meaningful by limiting opportunities for autonomy, dignity and recognition. In doing so, we extend current understanding of meaningful work by specifying how structural constraints give rise to passive agency, thereby systematically foreclosing access to meaningful work. We also clarify contingent conditions under which more active forms of agency may be enacted, and thus meaningful work can be sustained.

Scholars have proposed ethical principles and frameworks to support industry practitioners developing responsible AI. To enable these from theory to practice, a subset of research explores how practitioners actually enact abstract ethical concepts and guidance, surfacing factors that limit their efforts—e.g., organizational support—and informing ways to strengthen efforts towards safe and ethical AI in practice—e.g., practical checklists, educational workbooks. Curiously, this has been underexplored in relation to practitioners curating ethical datasets, the very foundation needed for fair ML technologies, despite the existence of various data ethics principles. It is unsurprising, then, that reports continue to emerge of ML datasets curated through questionable practices, including non-consensual web-scraping and exploitative labor practices. To address this gap, we describe the experiences of a project team curating FHIBE: a fair, human-centric benchmark dataset for computer vision technologies, grounded in recommendations by data ethics and fair ML scholars. Using an ethnographic lens, we share the team’s motivation and the set of principles FHIBE was based on, the challenges team members faced trying to execute multiple principles at once, and the ways they adapted in lieu of resources or insights from preceding scholarship. By tracing one team’s end-to-end data curation efforts, we offer new insights into practitioners’ realities translating data ethics, to inform valuable avenues for HCI and policy researchers to address in the future.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/CoVeR/.

The work is devoted to the development and testing of methods for intellectual decision-making support in the development of oil and gas fields in conditions of low situational awareness due to the variability of the geomagnetic situation and fragmented navigation data. The aim of the study is to reduce the risk of navigation errors during directional drilling by evaluating and proactively analyzing the variable component of errors in magnetic inclinometric measurements. The paper analyzes synchronized time sequences of solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field parameters obtained from satellite observations in the vicinity of the Lagrange point, as well as data from terrestrial geomagnetic observatories and the results of inclinometric measurements. A multi-stage data preprocessing procedure is proposed, including noise filtering, adaptive skip imputation, and time synchronization of satellite and terrestrial information sources. The decision support methodology is formalized as the task of comparing predicted deviations of magnetic declination and inclination with acceptable regulatory thresholds. The validation of the methodology was performed using the example of an extreme geomagnetic event 04/24/2023. It has been found that with intense variations in the geomagnetic field, the magnitude of the additional error of inclinometric measurements can increase to 1.45° in the angle of magnetic inclination and up to 6.04° in the magnetic declination. A comparative analysis of machine learning models has shown that the best quality of forecasting is provided by the random forest model, which demonstrates an average absolute error of 0.09-0.11° and a coefficient of determination of up to 0.70 when predicting magnetic inclination deviations. The results of the conducted research indicate the appropriateness of using the developed methodology as an algorithmic basis for intelligent decision support systems aimed at improving the safety and reliability of oil and gas field development processes.

LLM agents are increasingly given long, multi-step tasks to carry out, with the user reviewing little of what happens in between. Persistence, the tendency to keep working until a task is complete, is installed on purpose to improve performance on long tasks. Long-horizon tasks are typically complex, and the user's instruction can fall short of what the work actually requires, or conflict with the constraints the agent encounters in the task. We study what persistence does on long-horizon operations tasks that cannot be solved without breaking a documented constraint. We find that the agent pursues completion to the point of violating the constraint, and that a critically engaged user lowers the violation rate. Persistence takes violations from 29.2% to 58.3% across four models. Violations stay high wherever oversight goes quiet, whether the user is silent, assenting, or delegating with expressed trust. Only a questioning user, who asks for the basis of each action before allowing the next, brings the rate back to roughly the level measured without persistence. Practitioners should treat high persistence as a setting that carries a safety cost, and should recognize that the cost appears when oversight goes quiet. Safety here is better cast as a property of the human-AI pair than of the model alone. Project page: https://francis21c.github.io/quiet-oversight/
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Harmful language detection is commonly evaluated on broadly defined hate speech and toxicity benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether models that successfully detect harmful language in general can transfer this capability to more specific forms of hate. We investigate this problem for misogyny detection in Polish, an area for which dedicated resources remain scarce. We introduce a new dataset of Polish social media comments annotated for misogyny, gender-directed hateful speech. Using this resource, we first assess the reliability of LLM-assisted annotation and then evaluate general-to-specific transfer by comparing models trained on general harmful language data, safety-specialized models, and models fine-tuned directly for misogyny detection. Our results show that strong performance on general harmful language detection does not transfer uniformly to misogyny; safety-specialized models demonstrate substantially stronger generalization ability. The study contributes a new Polish resource for gender-directed harmful language and demonstrates that the scope and granularity of prior safety training are important factors in transferring harmful language detection from general to specific forms of hate.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Cybersickness remains one of the most persistent barriers to the widespread adoption of Virtual reality (VR), often causing nausea, dizziness, and visual discomfort that limit user engagement. This study proposes a machine learning-based adaptive adjustment framework that predicts and mitigates cybersickness in real time using only non-intrusive head-tracking data (HTD). The system dynamically adjusts the field of view (FoV) and fixed foveated rendering (FFR) parameters based on predicted discomfort levels, striking a balance between visual quality, system performance, and user comfort. A within-subjects experiment with 28 participants compared a baseline VR configuration with the adaptive system. A Gradient Boosting regressor achieved an average normalized prediction error of 1.84% on a six-participant held-out set, supporting preliminary feasibility of estimating cybersickness scores from kinematic features. With the adaptive module active, mean VRSQ scores were 27% lower and perceived cognitive workload 28% lower (both statistically significant), though the fixed, non-counterbalanced condition order means order or habituation effects may contribute. Average frame rates decreased modestly, indicating a trade-off between rendering performance and comfort. Overall, the results support real-time, sensor-driven adaptation as a lightweight approach for improving comfort in consumer VR systems without additional physiological sensors, pending counterbalanced, participant-disjoint validation.

Target-speaker automatic speech recognition (TS-ASR) is essential for reliable human-machine interaction in complex acoustic environments, where overlapping speech and background noise make it difficult to identify and recognize the intended speaker. Existing approaches typically rely on speaker enrollment or cascaded processing pipelines, limiting their flexibility in practical applications. To address these limitations, we propose an enrollment-free Speech-LLM framework that leverages wake-word text as a lexical cue to guide target-speaker recognition. Specifically, a text-cue encoder extracts lexical representations from the wake word, which are integrated into a pretrained speech encoder through cross-attention to establish an implicit association between the wake-word occurrence and the target speaker. This enables the model to selectively recognize subsequent commands from the target speaker without requiring enrollment speech or explicit wake-word boundaries. Furthermore, a large language model (LLM) unifies command transcription and non-target speaker rejection within a single autoregressive framework. To improve robustness against complex acoustic interference, we develop a large-scale speech synthesis and simulation pipeline with a progressive four-stage training strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a command character error rate of 16.15% and a non-target speaker rejection rate of 91.56%, yielding a unified score of 87.70%, compared with 71.70% for the strongest enrollment-free baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of wake-word-guided speaker selection and highlight the potential of integrating target-speaker recognition and rejection within a unified Speech-LLM framework for robust human-machine interaction.

Monte Carlo study of how silent LLM-scorer version updates bias within-person inference in longitudinal latent variable models (LGM/DSEM), and of version-aware / human-anchored corrections. Pure simulation; no external API calls, no human subjects.

Welding practicum requires students to maintain static postures for prolonged periods while controlling the electrode holder, which may impose biomechanical loads and increase the risk of musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). Nevertheless, welding instruction generally emphasizes weld quality, whereas the ergonomic risk experienced by the students receives limited attention. This study evaluated the ergonomic risk of students' working postures during a welding practicum at the Welding Laboratory, by comparing the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) and the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA). Subjective complaints were identified using the Nordic Body Map (NBM) questionnaire with 100 respondents, working postures were recorded on video from frontal and sagittal views, and body segment angles were extracted and scored. Because the postures adopted by the students were relatively uniform, two representative postures were analysed in depth, which are squatting and standing-bent forward. The total NBM scores were 52 for squatting and 65 for standing-bent forward, both in the moderate category, and most respondents reported pain in the neck, shoulder, back, and waist. The final RULA score was 7 for both postures, indicating that investigation and changes are required immediately. The final REBA scores were 11 for squatting (very high risk) and 7 for standing-bent forward (medium risk). Deep knee flexion and neck flexion in the squatting posture, together with trunk flexion of 50–70° and upper arm elevation relative to the trunk in both postures, were the dominant risk contributors, and the static and repetitive nature of the task increased the final scores. These findings suggest that the fixed-height working surface and the absence of posture guidance contribute to awkward working postures.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyze the impact of digital self-regulation deficit on the quality and productivity of Al-Qur'an memorization among students at Rumah Tahfiz Darul Aulia. The study employed a qualitative phenomenological approach with data collection techniques including observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation. Data analysis followed the interactive model of Miles and Huberman, comprising data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing. The results indicate that uncontrolled digital usage patterns among students characterized by prolonged duration, dominance of entertainment content, and usage during critical memorization periods significantly contribute to the emergence of self-regulation deficits. This deficit has a dual impact on students' tahfidz performance: in terms of memorization quality, it manifests as declining reading fluency, weakened memory retention, and reduced cognitive readiness during recitation sessions; and in terms of memorization productivity, it results in unmet daily ziyadah targets, inconsistent recitation schedules, and weakened intrinsic motivation. The study concludes that improving tahfidz performance in the digital era requires not only increasing memorization hours, but also strengthening students' self-regulation capacity to manage digital device use responsibly.

Objective: This scoping review will map how artificial intelligence (AI) is used to support learning, establishing and deepening mindfulness-based and mindfulness-informed (MBMI) practice, and which potentials and pitfalls are reported. Background: The effects of MBMI interventions depend on regular practice, but sustained engagement is difficult to achieve. AI applications that personalise, guide or monitor practice, or give feedback on it, are increasingly developed. Existing reviews are restricted to mindfulness-based interventions, to a single database or to questions of effectiveness. Inclusion criteria: Sources on people of any age who use, learn or teach MBMI practices (population) and on AI that delivers, guides, personalises or monitors practice or gives feedback on it to the practitioner (concept), in therapy, health promotion or prevention in any setting (context). Empirical studies of any design, development studies, reviews, conceptual papers and study protocols published in English or German are eligible. Methods: The review follows the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported according to PRISMA-ScR. MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycInfo, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library will be searched from inception. A human reviewer and a large language model (Claude, Anthropic) will screen records and chart data independently. Humans will decide all disagreements, and the human reviewer will verify every charted entry. Results will be summarised descriptively, in evidence maps and by directed qualitative content analysis, with the Behavior Change Resource Model and the Model of Engagement as deductive frameworks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Burnout syndrome is an emerging occupational health concern among university lecturers and may contribute to brain drain. This study examined the association between burnout syndrome and brain drain intention among university lecturers in Ilorin Metropolis, Nigeria. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 411 lecturers selected through multistage sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire incorporating selected Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) items. Of the questionnaires administered, 380 were retrieved (92.5% response rate). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and binary logistic regression at p < 0.05. The regression model adjusted for age, gender, marital status, academic rank, university type, and administrative duties. Results: Most respondents were male (85.5%), married (56.6%), and employed in federal universities (57.6%). Overall, 43.2% experienced high burnout syndrome, with emotional exhaustion being the predominant dimension (39.5%). Burnout reduced teaching effectiveness (75.0%), negatively affected health (79.4%), and increased job dissatisfaction (73.1%). More than half (59.4%) reported an intention to seek employment outside Nigeria. High burnout syndrome significantly predicted brain drain intention (AOR = 1.967; 95% CI: 1.184–3.268; p = 0.009). Conclusion: Burnout syndrome was significantly associated with brain drain intention among university lecturers. Institutional interventions that improve lecturers’ wellbeing, workload management, and staff welfare may support academic workforce retention in Nigerian universities.

Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness.
